market_context: United States; cooked dry pasta without sauce
title: White pasta vs. whole-wheat pasta: nutritional differences

seo.title: White pasta vs. whole-wheat pasta: nutritional differences
seo.meta_description: Whole-wheat pasta is not dramatically lower in calories, but it has about twice the fiber. Compare 149 vs. 158 calories and 3.9 vs. 1.8 g fiber per 100 g cooked.
seo.search_intent: Compare cooked white and whole-wheat pasta for calories, protein, carbohydrates, fiber and practical nutrition differences.

excerpt: Cooked without sauce, white and whole-wheat pasta are very similar in calories and protein. USDA references provide about 149 calories, 6.0 g protein and 3.9 g fiber per 100 g for whole-wheat pasta versus 158 calories, 5.8 g protein and 1.8 g fiber for enriched white pasta. Fiber is the meaningful gap.
content_html:
Whole-wheat pasta is sometimes treated as the low-calorie version of regular pasta, but that is not where the major nutritional difference lies. The calories are close; whole-wheat pasta's clearest advantage is fiber.

A cooked, like-for-like comparison

Using USDA entries for both foods in the cooked state keeps water content comparable:

Per 100 g cookedEnriched white pastaWhole-wheat pasta
Calories158 kcal149 kcal
Protein5.8 g6.0 g
Carbohydrate30.9 g30.1 g
Fiber1.8 g3.9 g

The calorie difference is only 9 calories per 100 g. Fiber, however, is more than doubled in the whole-wheat reference: 3.9 versus 1.8 g.

Why whole wheat has more fiber

Whole-wheat flour retains the bran and germ along with the endosperm. Refining removes much of those outer grain layers before white pasta is made.

Whole-grain pasta also tends to retain more of several naturally occurring minerals. Enriched white pasta has selected B vitamins and iron added back, so micronutrient comparisons are not as simple as “whole wheat has more of everything.”

Does whole-wheat pasta keep you fuller?

Its extra fiber can contribute to satiety, but the rest of the meal matters enormously. Vegetables, beans, meat, fish, eggs, cheese and the amount of added fat can change fullness more than the pasta choice alone.

A realistic serving shows the difference

At 180 g cooked, the references work out to roughly 284 calories and 3.2 g fiber for white pasta versus 268 calories and 7.0 g fiber for whole wheat. The fiber gap becomes meaningful while the calorie difference remains modest.

Which should you choose?

If increasing fiber and whole-grain intake is the goal, whole-wheat pasta has a clear edge. If you strongly prefer white pasta, it can still anchor a balanced meal. Choose for fiber, texture and the overall plate—not for a tiny calorie difference.

faq.question: Does whole-wheat pasta have far fewer calories?
faq.answer: No. The USDA references here differ by only 9 calories per 100 g cooked: 149 versus 158.

faq.question: Which pasta has more fiber?
faq.answer: Whole-wheat pasta, at about 3.9 g/100 g versus 1.8 g/100 g for the white pasta reference.

faq.question: Which has more protein?
faq.answer: They are essentially tied in these entries: 6.0 g versus 5.8 g per 100 g cooked.
